title: Release Strategies & Zero-Downtime Deploys
scopeHtml:
Scope: rolling, blue-green, canary, shadow, feature flags, expand/contract database migrations, rollback and automated canary analysis.

Scope: traffic shifting, shadow and A/B, mobile releases, config safety, regional waves, chaos engineering.

notes.title: Deployment strategies at a glance
notes.html:
How you put a new version in front of users decides how much damage a bad release can do.

Strategy How it works Rollback speed Extra cost Risk
Recreate stop old, start new slow, downtime none downtime
Rolling replace instances a few at a time medium low both versions live briefly
Blue-green full new stack beside the old, flip traffic instant (flip back) 2x capacity during switch DB changes
Canary send 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% of traffic to new fast (route back) small needs good metrics
Shadow copy real traffic to new version, discard its responses n/a extra compute no user impact

Worked example. A canary at 5% of 2M requests/hour is 100k requests, plenty to see a 2% error spike in 3-5 minutes, while the other 95% of users never noticed.

Industry examples. Netflix (Spinnaker + Kayenta automated canary analysis), Google and Facebook canary through staged regions, Amazon deploys one "cell" or region at a time.

Everyday analogy. Testing a new recipe on one table before changing the whole menu.

Common interview traps.

  • "Rolling and canary are the same." Rolling is about how instances are replaced; canary is about how much traffic you expose and judging by metrics.
  • Blue-green doubles cost and still needs a plan for the shared database.

notes.title: Rolling updates in detail
notes.html:
In Kubernetes, a Deployment's maxSurge (extra pods allowed above desired) and maxUnavailable (pods allowed below desired) control the pace. With replicas: 10, maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0, new pods are created in batches; each must pass readiness before an old pod is terminated, so capacity never drops.

Things that make rolling updates safe: good readiness probes, graceful shutdown (handle SIGTERM, finish in-flight requests, preStop hook, terminationGracePeriodSeconds), and backward-compatible versions, because v1 and v2 serve traffic simultaneously.

Worked example. Without graceful shutdown, a pod killed mid-request returns 502s. The fix: on SIGTERM stop accepting new connections, wait up to 30 s for in-flight requests, then exit; plus a short preStop: sleep 5 so the load balancer deregisters the pod first.

Industry examples. Kubernetes default is rolling; ECS and AWS Auto Scaling "instance refresh" do the same.

Everyday analogy. Replacing the tyres of a car one at a time while it keeps rolling, versus lifting the whole car.

Common interview traps.

  • Readiness probe returning OK before the app can actually serve (cache not warm), so errors go to users.
  • Incompatible API or DB change makes v1 and v2 conflict mid-rollout.

notes.title: Blue-green and feature flags
notes.html:
Blue-green: two identical environments. Blue serves users; you deploy and test Green; then switch the router/load balancer to Green. Rollback is switching back. Great for big atomic changes and quick recovery; costs double capacity for a while.

Feature flags (toggles) separate deploy (code in production) from release (users see it). New code ships dark; you turn it on for staff, then 1%, then everyone, and turn it off in seconds without redeploying. Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, Statsig, homegrown.

Flag hygiene: short lifetime (delete after rollout), owner, default safe value, test both states. Old flags become technical debt and combinatorial test cases.

Industry examples. Facebook "Gatekeeper", Netflix and Uber use flags for gradual exposure; Knight Capital (2012) lost about $440M in 45 minutes partly because a deployment left old code and a reused flag active on one of eight servers: a lesson about partial deploys and flag reuse.

Everyday analogy. A stage curtain: the set is built behind it (deploy), and you open the curtain later (release).

Common interview traps.

  • Flags that never get removed.
  • Treating a flag flip as risk-free: it is still a production change; log and alert on it.

notes.title: Databases and zero-downtime migrations
notes.html:
Code rolls back easily; data does not. Use the expand/contract (parallel change) pattern so every step is compatible with both old and new code:

  1. Expand: add the new column/table (nullable, no default lock), deploy code that writes to both.
  2. Migrate: backfill old rows in small batches.
  3. Switch: read from the new column.
  4. Contract: much later, remove the old column once no version uses it.

Never rename or drop a column in the same release that stops using it. Avoid long locks: on big tables use online schema tools (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change, Postgres CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY).

-- step 1: expand (safe, backward compatible)
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text;
-- step 2: backfill in batches
UPDATE users SET full_name = first_name || ' ' || last_name
 WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND full_name IS NULL;
-- step 4 (a later release): contract
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN first_name;

Worked example. An ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT that rewrites a 500M-row table in older MySQL locks writes for minutes; a nullable add plus batched backfill never blocks.

Industry examples. GitHub's gh-ost and Stripe's online migration practices are well-known; Stripe calls out dual-writing and shadow reads for data moves.

Everyday analogy. Building the new bridge beside the old one, moving traffic, and only then demolishing the old bridge.

Common interview traps.

  • Migration that runs automatically at app start on every replica, racing against itself.
  • A migration with no rollback path (drop column) in the same deploy as the code change.

notes.title: Rollback, roll-forward and automated judgement
notes.html:
Rollback returns to the previous artifact; it works when the change is backward compatible (no destructive migration). Roll forward ships a quick fix instead; sometimes safer when data has already changed. Decide in advance which is allowed.

Mature teams automate the decision: progressive delivery tools (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker with Kayenta) compare canary metrics (error rate, p99 latency, saturation) to the baseline and promote or abort automatically. Define SLO-based rollback triggers, e.g. "abort if 5xx rate is above 1% for 3 minutes or p99 up 30%".

Worked example. Argo Rollouts steps: 5% for 5 min → analysis passes → 25% → 100%. If the Prometheus query rate(http_5xx)/rate(http_total) < 0.01 fails, the rollout aborts and traffic returns to the stable ReplicaSet automatically.

Industry examples. Google's SRE practice: most outages are caused by changes, so automated canary analysis and fast rollback are a primary defense.

Everyday analogy. A smoke alarm wired to the sprinklers: no person has to notice first.

Common interview traps.

  • Rollback plan that was never tested.
  • Judging a canary by CPU only; use user-facing metrics (errors, latency, business KPIs).

notes.title: How traffic is actually shifted
notes.html:
"Send 5% to v2" must be implemented somewhere. Mechanisms:

  • Load balancer weights (AWS ALB weighted target groups, NGINX/HAProxy upstream weights).
  • Kubernetes: two Deployments behind one Service gives only crude ratio by pod count; use Argo Rollouts/Flagger with an Ingress or mesh for exact weights.
  • Service mesh (Istio VirtualService, Linkerd): percent- or header-based routing.
  • DNS weighted records (Route 53): coarse, slow because of caching and TTLs.
  • Feature flags / application level: choose by user ID hash so the same user always sees the same version.
# Argo Rollouts canary steps
strategy:
  canary:
    steps:
      - setWeight: 5
      - pause: { duration: 5m }
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause: { duration: 10m }
      - setWeight: 100

Sticky canaries matter: if a user flips between v1 and v2 on every request, sessions and caches behave oddly. Hash on user or session ID.

Industry examples. Netflix Spinnaker, Google's internal rollout system, Envoy-based mesh routing at Lyft and Airbnb.

Everyday analogy. A tap with a precise dial versus swapping the whole tap at once.

Common interview traps.

  • DNS-based canary expecting instant control; TTLs make it slow and imprecise.
  • Random per-request routing breaking multi-step user flows.

notes.title: Dark launches, A/B tests and shadow traffic
notes.html:
Three related but different ideas:

  • Dark launch: new code runs in production but its result is not shown to users (compare outputs silently).
  • Shadow / mirrored traffic: copy real requests to the new version, discard its responses, compare with the old one. Side effects (emails, payments, DB writes) must be disabled or sandboxed.
  • A/B test: expose variants to user groups to measure a product metric (conversion), with statistical significance. It tests ideas; canary tests safety.

Worked example. Rewriting a pricing engine: shadow-run the new one on 100% of requests for a week, log any price differences, fix them, and only then switch 1% of users.

Industry examples. GitHub's "Scientist" library compares old and new code paths in production; Netflix and Booking.com run thousands of A/B tests.

Everyday analogy. A flight simulator running alongside the real flight, comparing the pilot's choices without moving the plane.

Common interview traps.

  • Shadow traffic that sends duplicate emails or charges customers.
  • Confusing canary (is it safe?) with A/B (is it better?).

notes.title: Mobile and client-side releases
notes.html:
Clients cannot be rolled back by you. Controls: staged rollout in the store (1% → 5% → 20% → 100%, halt on bad crash rate), crash-free session thresholds (for example above 99.5%) monitored via Crashlytics, server-side feature flags / remote config to disable a broken feature without a new build, minimum supported version and force-update prompts, and API backward compatibility for old app versions that stay in the wild for months.

Worked example. Version 5.2 crashes on Android 12 devices. Halting the rollout at 8% limits damage; a remote-config kill switch disables the crashing screen for the already-updated users while a 5.2.1 fix is reviewed.

Industry examples. Instagram, Uber and Swiggy rely on remote config and staged rollouts; Play Console and App Store Connect both support phased release.

Everyday analogy. A printed book: once sent to readers you cannot edit their copies, so you add an errata slip service (remote config) and release in batches.

Common interview traps.

  • Breaking the API for old clients, which keep calling it for months.
  • No kill switch for risky features.

notes.title: Safe configuration changes
notes.html:
Many of the largest outages came from a configuration change pushed everywhere at once, not code. Treat config like code: version it, review it, validate it (schema checks), and roll it out progressively (canary by region or cell) with automatic rollback. Separate static config baked at deploy from dynamic config changed live, and make dynamic changes auditable with a log of who changed what.

Worked example. A malformed rate-limit rule pushed to all regions at once blocks all traffic for 25 minutes. A progressive rollout would have broken one region and been rolled back in 2 minutes.

Industry examples. Public incident reviews from Cloudflare, Facebook (2021 BGP outage) and Google Cloud highlight global config pushes without staging or fast rollback.

Everyday analogy. Test a new street-light timing on one intersection before changing the whole city.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating config as "not a deploy" and skipping review and canary.
  • Config systems with no history, so nobody knows what changed.

notes.title: Multi-region and cell-based rollout
notes.html:
At scale, roll out in waves: one-box (a single instance) → one cell/region → a few regions → all, with a bake time (soak period) between waves and automatic halts on alarms. Cell-based architecture partitions users into independent cells so a bad deploy or failure affects only one cell. Avoid deploying to all regions simultaneously; prefer low-traffic regions first.

Wave 1: 1 instance (one-box)     bake 30 min
Wave 2: 1 small region           bake 1 h
Wave 3: 3 regions                bake 1 h
Wave 4: everything else

Worked example. A bug present only for accounts with more than 10,000 items shows up in wave 2 (one region), affecting 2% of users, instead of everyone.

Industry examples. Amazon's deployment guidelines (one-box, wave-based, automatic rollback on alarms) and Google's staged global rollouts are the model.

Everyday analogy. Opening a new drug in clinical phases rather than giving it to the whole country.

Common interview traps.

  • Deploying to all regions at once "to save time".
  • Bake time too short to expose slow leaks or daily-cycle problems.

notes.title: Chaos engineering and game days
notes.html:
Prove that failure handling works before real failures. Chaos engineering injects controlled faults (kill pods or instances, add latency, drop a dependency, fail a zone) into production or a production-like environment, with a hypothesis ("checkout stays above 99.9% if one cache node dies") and a small blast radius. Game days rehearse incident response and rollback, including restoring from backups.

Tools: Chaos Monkey, Litmus, Chaos Mesh, Gremlin, AWS Fault Injection Service.

Worked example. A team kills the primary database in staging and discovers the app does not reconnect: connection pools keep dead connections. They fix timeouts and retry logic before it happens at 2 a.m.

Industry examples. Netflix created Chaos Monkey and the Simian Army; Amazon and Google run regular DiRT or game-day exercises.

Everyday analogy. A fire drill: you find out the exit is blocked when it is a drill, not a fire.

Common interview traps.

  • Chaos with no hypothesis, monitoring or abort button.
  • Never testing restore from backup; an untested backup is a hope.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Pick a strategy by risk and cost: recreate (downtime), rolling (default, needs graceful shutdown and compatible versions), blue-green (instant switch, double cost), canary (small exposure judged by metrics), shadow (zero user impact). Feature flags separate deploy from release and must be cleaned up. Database changes use expand/contract and online migrations so old and new code coexist. Prefer fast rollback or roll-forward decided in advance, and automate promotion and abort with SLO-based canary analysis.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common release-engineering question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Rolling replaces instances gradually in place. Blue-green runs a full second environment and flips traffic at once, so rollback is flipping back, at the price of double capacity. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version and promotes it only if metrics look good, limiting the blast radius.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Rolling is the Kubernetes default and cheap but both versions run during the update, so they must be compatible. Blue-green suits big atomic switches; the database is shared, so schema changes still need care. Canary needs good metrics and enough traffic to be statistically meaningful. Shadow (traffic mirroring) tests with real traffic and no user impact but needs idempotent or discarded side effects.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing up rolling (how instances are replaced) with canary (how much traffic and judged by metrics).
  • Forgetting blue-green's database problem.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which is the safest? → Canary with automated analysis.
  2. How big should the first canary slice be? → Small but statistically sufficient; for 2M requests/hour, 5% is 100k requests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior chooses based on risk, cost and observability maturity.

questions.promptHtml: Users see 502 errors during every rolling update. What could be wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A real day-to-day issue that tests Kubernetes lifecycle knowledge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Pods are being terminated while still receiving requests. Fix with graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM by finishing in-flight requests, add a preStop sleep so the load balancer deregisters the pod first, set a sufficient terminationGracePeriodSeconds, and make sure readiness only passes when the app can really serve.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: On delete, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and concurrently removes the pod from Service endpoints; the propagation takes a moment, so requests can still arrive. With maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge > 0 capacity never dips. Keep-alive connections from a load balancer need draining too.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• App ignores SIGTERM and gets SIGKILLed after 30 seconds.
  • Readiness passes before caches or connections are warm.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is PID 1 relevant? → Signals may not reach the app if a shell wrapper is PID 1.
  2. What about long requests/WebSockets? → Longer grace period and connection draining.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the endpoint propagation race and tunes drain settings.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between deploying and releasing, and how do feature flags help?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the decoupling idea behind modern delivery.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Deploy means the code is running in production; release means users can use the feature. Flags let you ship code dark, enable it for staff, then a percentage, then everyone, and turn it off in seconds without redeploying, which also enables trunk-based development.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Costs: flags are branching logic in production, need tests for both states, and become debt if never removed. Practice: owners, expiry dates, safe defaults when the flag service is down, audit logs, and treating a flag flip as a production change that can be alerted on. Knight Capital (2012) is the cautionary tale of partially deployed code and a reused flag.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Never deleting flags.
  • Flag service outage that defaults to "on" for risky features.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Flags vs config? → Flags change behaviour per user/segment dynamically; config sets static parameters.
  2. How do you test? → Both states in CI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior brings up lifecycle management and failure modes of the flag system.

questions.promptHtml: How do you rename a database column with zero downtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who have done live migrations from those who haven't.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Never rename in one step. Use expand/contract: add the new column; deploy code that writes to both; backfill old rows in small batches; switch reads to the new column; and only in a later release drop the old column when no running version uses it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
During a rolling or canary rollout old and new code coexist, so every schema state must work with both. A direct RENAME breaks the old code instantly. For large tables avoid long locks: add nullable columns, create indexes concurrently (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres), and use online schema tools such as gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change on MySQL.

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text;          -- expand
UPDATE users SET full_name = first_name || ' ' || last_name
 WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND full_name IS NULL;  -- backfill in batches
-- later release: ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN first_name;  -- contract

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Migration run on every pod startup, racing itself.
  • Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it, blocking rollback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you roll back? → Rollback is possible until the contract step, which is why it is delayed.
  2. What about a huge backfill? → Throttle batches, monitor replica lag and locks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions replica lag, lock behaviour and dual-write consistency checks.

questions.promptHtml: How would you automate canary promotion and rollback?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows progressive delivery maturity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use a progressive delivery controller (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker with Kayenta) that shifts traffic in steps and queries metrics at each step, such as 5xx rate and p99 latency compared with the baseline. If the analysis fails, it aborts and returns traffic to the stable version; if it passes, it promotes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Define explicit thresholds from SLOs, for example abort if 5xx exceeds 1% for 3 minutes. Compare canary to baseline (not just absolute numbers) so seasonal traffic does not mislead. Use user-facing and business metrics, not CPU only. Make sure enough traffic hits the canary for the signal to be statistically meaningful, and have a manual override.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Judging only on infrastructure metrics.
  • Promoting before enough data (low-traffic canary).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Rollback or roll forward? → Rollback if backward compatible; roll forward if data already changed.
  2. Where do you test the rollback path? → Regularly in staging and game days.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs metric comparison, sample size and failure handling for the analysis itself.

questions.contextHtml: At 14:02 a deploy goes to 100% of a checkout service. By 14:05 the 5xx rate rises from 0.2% to 6%, p99 latency doubles, and support tickets begin. The release included a code change and a database migration that dropped an unused-looking column.
questions.promptHtml: You are on call. What do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts reading code to find the bug before mitigating.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did anything change besides the deploy? Is the error tied to a version? Can the previous version still read the schema?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Declare an incident, roll back the application version now (or flip the feature flag) after checking the migration did not break the old code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The new code bug; a dependency/config difference; the migration (column dropped but still used by old paths).
  4. How I'd verify: Compare error logs by version, traces of failing requests, deploy and migration timeline.
  5. Root cause: The migration contracted too early; the old code path still referenced the column.
  6. Fix: Restore the column from backup or re-add it, roll back code, then redo using expand/contract across two releases.
  7. Prevention: Block destructive migrations in the same release as code changes, use canary with automated analysis, rehearse rollbacks.
  8. Trade-offs: Rolling back first costs a bit of time but ends user pain; deep diagnosis waits until after.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Data already written in the new format? → Roll forward with a compatibility shim.
  • Why was this not caught in staging? → Staging data and traffic differ; add canary and production-like tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team finished a post-mortem showing 80% of their incidents followed a change; they added automatic canary analysis and halved time to restore.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: debugs live without mitigation.
  • Hire: rolls back quickly, communicates, finds cause.
  • Strong hire: handles the migration trap, prevention and process.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement a 5% canary in practice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you know the mechanics, not only the buzzword.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use weighted routing at a load balancer, ingress or service mesh, driven by a progressive delivery tool (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) that steps the weight and checks metrics. Make routing sticky by hashing on user or session so a user does not flip between versions. DNS weights are coarse and slow because of TTLs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Two Deployments behind one Service give only a ratio by pod count; exact weights need an ingress or mesh. Application-level flags can choose by user ID hash. Argo Rollouts expresses steps such as setWeight: 5, pause: 5m, then analysis.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting DNS-based canaries to be instant and precise.
  • Random per-request routing that breaks multi-step flows.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do metrics come from? → Prometheus queries in an AnalysisTemplate.
  2. Header-based routing? → Route internal testers to v2 by header.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions stickiness and metric comparison against the baseline.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a canary, shadow traffic and an A/B test?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates often blur safety testing and product experimentation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A canary tests safety by giving a small share of real users the new version and watching error and latency metrics. Shadow traffic copies real requests to the new version and discards its responses, so users are unaffected. An A/B test measures a product metric such as conversion between variants with statistical significance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Shadowing needs side effects (emails, payments, writes) disabled or sandboxed. Dark launches run code in production without showing results. GitHub's Scientist library compares old and new code paths.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Shadow traffic that sends duplicate emails or charges.
  • Calling a canary an A/B test.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When use shadowing? → Rewrites of critical logic such as pricing.
  2. How do you compare outputs? → Log differences and review mismatches.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs safe comparison and statistical rigour.

questions.promptHtml: Why are configuration changes a leading cause of outages and how do you make them safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many famous outages were config pushes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Config often bypasses review, tests and staged rollout, yet a bad value can take everything down at once. Treat config like code: version it, review it, validate against a schema, roll it out progressively (one cell or region first), watch SLOs, and be able to roll it back in seconds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Separate static config baked at deploy from dynamic config changed live, and audit every dynamic change. Facebook's 2021 outage and several Cloudflare incidents involved global changes without staging.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "It is only config" so no canary.
  • No history of who changed what.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you validate? → Schema and policy checks in CI plus dry-runs.
  2. Rollback? → Previous version restored automatically on alarm.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior builds progressive rollout and auto-rollback into the config system.

questions.promptHtml: How would you roll out a change across many regions safely?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests blast-radius thinking.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In waves: one-box (a single instance), then one small region or cell, then a few regions, then the rest, with a bake time between waves and automatic halt on alarms. A cell-based architecture limits any failure to one cell. Start with low-traffic regions and never deploy everywhere at once.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Bake time must be long enough to catch slow leaks and daily-cycle issues. Each wave has gates on SLO metrics. This is the model used in Amazon-style deployment guidelines.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Deploying to all regions simultaneously to save time.
  • Bake times too short to expose problems.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What halts a wave? → Alarms on errors, latency or saturation.
  2. How do you handle global state? → Backward-compatible schema and staged data migrations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs cells, waves and gates together.

questions.promptHtml: What is chaos engineering and how do you do it safely?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows reliability mindset.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Deliberately injecting controlled failures (kill pods, add latency, drop a dependency, fail a zone) to verify the system handles them. Start with a hypothesis, a small blast radius, monitoring and an abort button, and run in staging first before production. Game days rehearse incident response and restores.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Tools: Chaos Monkey, Litmus, Chaos Mesh, Gremlin, AWS Fault Injection Service. Typical discoveries: connection pools not reconnecting after a database failover, missing timeouts and retries, single points of failure.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Chaos with no hypothesis or abort criteria.
  • Never testing restore from backup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why in production? → Real traffic and dependencies expose issues staging cannot.
  2. First experiment? → Kill one instance during normal load.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links experiments to SLOs and fixes findings.

questions.contextHtml: Version 5.2 of your Android app is at 8% staged rollout. Crashlytics shows crash-free sessions at 97.1% (baseline 99.6%), concentrated on Android 12 devices when opening the payments screen. Reviews are dropping. A fix will take two days including store review.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Continues the rollout while preparing a fix.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the crash from this version only? Is there a feature flag around the screen? Can the server detect the version?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout; disable the payments entry point for 5.2 users via remote config or flag; show a fallback or web flow.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A change in the payments SDK or a library incompatible with Android 12; a config mismatch; a backend contract change.
  4. How I'd verify: Crashlytics stack traces by OS/device, the diff of 5.1 to 5.2, reproduce on an Android 12 emulator.
  5. Root cause: Whatever the stack trace shows, for example a null from a changed API response on Android 12.
  6. Fix: Patch, ship 5.2.1 as an expedited release, resume staged rollout.
  7. Prevention: Test matrix including API levels, automated rollout gates on crash-free rate, kill switches for every risky feature.
  8. Trade-offs: Disabling the feature loses revenue short term; it is better than crashing users.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• No remote kill switch exists → force-update prompt for 5.2 after 5.2.1 ships, and add switches going forward.
  • Backend can help? → Make the API tolerate the failing path.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A remote-config kill switch reduced crash impact within 10 minutes while the fix went through store review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
